dialogue.literal_gloss: Kurova [to / at rova] • guva [guva] • yaiva [yaiva] • tsika [tsika] • yakakosha [it (past) kosha] • yekudzosa [yekudzosa] • mweya [mweya] • wemufi [wemufi] • mumusha [in / singular musha]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakakosha')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakakosha' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mumusha')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mumusha'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('Kurova')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'Kurova' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: The Traditional Memorial Ceremony ('Kurova Guva' / 'Magadziko')
cultural_notes.content: In traditional Shona heritage, 'kurova guva' (also called 'magadziko' or 'chenura') was a solemn ceremony held about a year after an adult's passing to end the mourning period and symbolically welcome their protective ancestral spirit back to watch over the family homestead ('mumusha').

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: How do you form ordinal numbers like 'first', 'second', and 'third' in Shona?
options: Place the word 'nhamba' after the verb
Attach '-ekutanga' (first), '-echipiri' (second), and '-echitatu' (third) with the noun's possessive prefix
active_exercises.correct_answer: Attach '-ekutanga' (first), '-echipiri' (second), and '-echitatu' (third) with the noun's possessive prefix
active_exercises.explanation: Ordinal numbers use '-ekutanga' (1st), '-echipiri' (2nd), '-echitatu' (3rd), e.g., 'zuva rechitatu' ('the third day').
